tells: Silhouette chase choreography moves through very different settings: park gate, docks, a purple alley seen from overhead, a hypnotic spiral, a moonlit rooftop and a harbour with a rocket. Each scene clearly continues the one before it.
Each frame uses a different bold palette (dusty pink, teal and ochre, violet and green, acid lime, peach against black, slate blue), so the sequence has a real colour score.
The credits are built into the scenes: a title on the park arch, a name lying in perspective on the alley floor. They are not laid on top like slides.
Paper grain, cast shadows and the pool of light under a street lamp give the flat-cel style depth.
The animation has a character language: Snowy is white against black figures, and the chase gags and the spiral push the story forward.
gaps: The end-credit type goes back to a plain sans block, which is weaker than the title cards set into the scenes; the type could keep its period character all the way through.
A few compositions, like the rooftop chase in front of the moon, are the expected genre move; one more truly unexpected staging would lift it.
The silhouette-caper approach owes a clear debt to 60s title design; it could push harder past homage into its own visual language.

tells: The idea belongs only to this piece: a mechanical clockwork map that builds the world, so the opening also orients viewers to the geography of the story.
The materials are rich: engraved metal on the armillary band, wood and brass gears, a tilt-shift miniature feel, and warm sunlight blooming from the sphere.
The choreography is clear: a dive through the armillary, cities unfolding mechanically, a cut down to the flat map, then a pull back to the title band. The camera has weight and a sense of travel.
The credits use a carefully chosen engraved serif in small caps, each with a heraldic sigil icon. They are placed in the miniature scene at a deliberate small scale.
The title lockup sits inside the sculpted band with dragons, so the bookends rhyme with the opening frame.
gaps: The palette stays in one warm sepia and bronze range; a little more colour contrast between regions could strengthen the storytelling.
The credit type is small and sometimes fights the busy detail behind it (the Michelle Fairley card, for example), so it reads less clearly.
The flat-map interstitial is a little less finished than the 3D miniatures around it.

tells: The idea is witty and only works for this film: each credit is set as its own fictional cigarette-pack design, which fits the film's satire of tobacco branding.

The typography has a strong point of view. Each name gets a different period-accurate packaging lettering: a ribbon banner, a brush script, an engraved serif with 'LIGHTS', a sunburst filter label, a deco menthol face, and a 'Written for the screen' script set against a row of filters.
Real print texture: off-register flat colour, paper grain and embossed gold rules all suggest scanned packaging.
The palette changes on purpose from pack to pack (royal blue and gold, orange and cream, Americana stripes, red, mint green) while staying inside one period system.
Tight crops make every frame read like a packaging detail and a poster at once.
gaps: The motion implied by the frames is mostly slides and pans across flat surfaces, so it has less camera choreography and weight than the best entry.
The structure repeats (a crop of a pack plus a name), and nothing breaks the pattern for surprise until the cigarette-row card.
It has less depth and light than B; folding in real 3D pack geometry or cellophane highlights in places would add dimension.

tells: The idea belongs only to this show: the map of the world as a clockwork mechanism, with cities that build themselves, so the credits work as an orientation device
Real material work: aged brass, carved wood, engraved metal bands with heraldic relief, parchment cartography
The light is motivated: a central sun burns through the armillary sphere and raking light falls on the miniature cities, with a strong range from glare to shadow
The frames change type, from close macro on the engraved band to a high wide over the city, a cog-driven tower and a top-down map, which implies choreographed camera flight and mechanical motion
Credits are set in a classical Trajan-like serif with small sigils, placed inside the 3D space rather than laid on top
The palette of burnished gold, verdigris and smoke is restrained and consistent; the logo bookends the piece with the same sun-band motif
gaps: The credit type is a well-worn epic-fantasy classical serif; a more particular face would match the originality of the image
A few credits sit in murky low-contrast areas and lose legibility

defects: Brick texture tiles visibly and repeats on large wall planes; the walls are flat boxes with no edge wear, no normal or parallax depth, and simple block geometry with no props or set dressing
The signs float on the walls with no mounting hardware and no light spill or bounce onto the brick; the boxes look pasted on rather than lit into the scene
Too many frames are crushed to near-black: the left halves of shots and the roofline are dead areas with no detail
The whip-pan blur smears the credit text until it can't be read (the 'Mira ...' sign and the second 'Written & Directed By' frame), so credits are lost in transit
The title uses a different fill for every letter (halftone, stripes, LED dots, neon outline, solid, RGB-split) with no shared system, so it reads as a sampler rather than a design
The ending turns letters off ('N GHT HO S') and the piece fades out with no final lockup, so it reads as a glitch rather than a resolve
The soundtrack is band-limited at about 19.5 kHz with a static low drone and the same transient repeated about every 0.3 s; it sounds like a loop-based or generated bed, not a scored mix
The 4.2 s title hold has almost no in-shot motion apart from flicker
gaps: Choreography: every credit uses the same move (dolly past a wall sign, then a whip pan), with no variation in camera language, scale or rhythm and no motivated transitions that carry one sign into the next. Top studios would build a camera path that grows and pays off, not a carousel.

Finish and world-building: the alley is a gray-box-level asset with tiling brick, no atmosphere volume, no wet-ground reflections, no light falloff from the signs onto their surroundings and no secondary detail. The neon-sign premise needs glow and haze to sell it, and both are missing.

Sound and payoff: the click grid is regular and the riser and drop at about 7–8.5 s land the title, but the soundtrack has no motif, no sound design tied to the signs (buzz, relay clunk, flicker crackle) and no settling tail. Neither the title nor the flicker-off ending gets a sonic or visual button that rhymes with the opening.
